overview: The atlas's “East Java” is a regional shelf, not the name of one medieval country and not the modern Indonesian province described by its imported summary. The exact id spans 1000 to 1279, but its four-part polygon is stranger than its label. It includes tested Kediri, Malang, Central Javanese Yogyakarta and Semarang, southern Borneo's Banjarmasin, and Bima on Sumbawa. It excludes tested Janggala or Sidoarjo, Surabaya, Gresik, Tuban, Madura, Bali, Lombok, and Sumbawa Besar. In real East Javanese geography, mountains and the Brantas helped distinguish upper-valley Kediri from lower-river Janggala and upland Singhasari. Political authority changed from late Mataram or Isana through Airlangga's Kahuripan, Janggala and Panjalu or Kediri, then Singhasari. Those were related histories, not one state wearing a 279-year nametag. The final atlas click deepens the error: at 1279 it relabels the same tested footprint “Kediri.” Historical Kediri's dominant period had ended by 1222, a 57-year lag, while Singhasari or Tumapel continued until 1292. This card uses the layer as a regional doorway and keeps map membership distinct from sovereignty, language, ethnicity, or everyday uniformity.

periods.title: 1000 to 1016: Dharmavamsa and a remembered rupture
periods.summary: Dharmawangsa or Dharmavamsa appears in the Pucangan charter as Airlangga’s royal kinsman. The 1041 text later claims that his city suddenly burned and Airlangga fled. Because this is a retrospective victory narrative shaped by court rhetoric, it cannot identify every attacker, victim, cause, or consequence of the remembered 1016 rupture.

periods.title: 1016 to 1019: survival after court destruction
periods.summary: A broad political synthesis places Airlangga’s succession after the violent end of Dharmawangsa’s court, but evidence for 1016 to 1019 is thin. That gap should be presented as an uncertain interval in royal recovery, not proof that settlements, agriculture, worship, or exchange vanished across the region.

periods.title: 1019 to 1037: Airlangga rebuilds royal power
periods.summary: Airlangga gradually established authority, fought opponents, patronized religion and literature, and became the royal subject of the Pucangan inscription and Arjunawiwaha tradition. These court sources celebrate restoration. They cannot prove that one ruler controlled the atlas polygon or that recovery benefited every community equally.

periods.title: 1037 to 1042: dam work, boats, and succession
periods.summary: The 1037 Kamalagyan record describes a dam built where Brantas flooding damaged fields and interrupted boat traffic. Water control joined royal action to local labor and maintenance. Airlangga later retired, and traditions remember a division of authority, but the mechanism and exact boundary remain debated.

periods.title: 1042 to 1052: Janggala and Panjalu take shape
periods.summary: Later scholarship commonly describes Janggala near the lower Brantas and Panjalu or Kadiri farther upriver. New readings warn that these names and territories changed and that 1042 was not a perfectly documented border-drawing ceremony. The first post-Airlangga years remain a reconstruction from uneven inscriptions.

periods.title: 1052 to 1117: rival centers and a thin record
periods.summary: Janggala and Panjalu appear through scattered charters and later histories rather than a continuous royal diary. Panjalu eventually became more visible, while the lower Brantas retained its own political importance. Gaps in inscriptions should stay gaps; they do not justify invented rulers, borders, wars, or silent uniformity.

periods.title: 1117 to 1135: Bameswara and formal grants
periods.summary: Padlegan I names Bameswara in 1117, and the 1120 Panumbangan order records a sima grant. These dated inscriptions make Panjalu administration clearer through selected privileges, obligations, officials, and witnesses. They still document exceptional transactions rather than every tax, village, household, or political boundary.

periods.title: 1135 to 1157: Jayabhaya, victory, and poetry
periods.summary: Jayabhaya’s 1135 Hantang inscription carries the formula “Panjalu is victorious.” In 1157, Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh completed the Bharatayuddha under his patronage. The slogan does not reveal a whole campaign, while the poem shows creative Old Javanese scholarship rather than a literal battlefield transcript.

periods.title: 1157 to 1222: later Kediri courts and Kertajaya
periods.summary: Later rulers sponsored charters, sacred places, and kakawin associated with East Javanese court culture. The manuscripts read today are often later copies, especially from Bali. In 1222 Ken Angrok defeated Kertajaya and established new authority around Tumapel or Singhasari; that political transfer did not make Kediri’s settlements or cultural traditions disappear.

periods.title: 1222 to 1279: Singhasari replaces Kediri power
periods.summary: Ken Angrok’s victory opened Singhasari rule centered near Malang. Records for its rulers conflict, so later chronicle intrigue cannot be pasted into a seamless biography. Wisnuwardhana died in 1268, Kertanagara followed, and Singhasari continued past the atlas endpoint until 1292. The 1279 relabeling is therefore late and wrong.

sections.title: Audit the exact label, shape, and seams

items.text: The exact record is id “east-java,” label “East Java,” indexed circa 1000 to 1279 from historical basemaps. Coverage reports three border files and no deep card. Its imported summary instead describes the modern Indonesian province, so that text cannot identify the medieval layer or repair its chronology and shape.

At 1000 the target is one MultiPolygon with four components, four rings, 153 decoded positions, and bounds from about 109.115 to 118.983 degrees east and 9.178 degrees south to 1.369 degrees south. Those exact measurements audit a software object. They do not establish a medieval border.

The 1100 and 1200 snapshots share a second geometry: four components, four rings, and 152 positions. Their tested members are Kediri, Kelud, Trowulan, Singhasari, Malang, Blitar, Madiun, Yogyakarta, Semarang, Banjarmasin, and Bima. Stability across two files proves repetition, not political accuracy.

The same polygon excludes tested Janggala or Sidoarjo, Surabaya, Tuban, Gresik, Pamekasan on Madura, Denpasar, Mataram on Lombok, and Sumbawa Besar. A layer called East Java therefore omits key East Javanese coast and delta points while reaching Central Java, Borneo, and eastern Sumbawa.

At 900, tested Java points belonged to mataram while Banjarmasin and Bima belonged to malay. At 1279, all eleven target-member points abruptly belong to kediri, and that assignment persists at 1300. Neither click marks one historical founding or fall; both are editorial seams in coarse data.

sections.title: Follow courts, conflict, and communities through change

items.text: The 1041 Pucangan charter remembers Dharmavamsa inviting Airlangga to a royal wedding, then says the city turned to ashes and Airlangga went to the forest with Narottama. It is a later royal commemoration shaped like epic history. The burning points to warfare, loss, and flight, but the text cannot count affected households.

Airlangga rebuilt royal authority after the rupture and patronized a court in which Mpu Kanwa composed Arjunawiwaha. His story joins diplomacy, kinship, warfare, religion, and literature. Court praise magnifies the king, however, so it cannot measure how farmers, captives, port workers, or rival communities experienced consolidation.

Janggala and Panjalu or Kediri are useful names for post-Airlangga political centers, often associated with lower and upper Brantas regions. Recent epigraphic work warns that the labels, dates, and spatial relationship shifted. A neat two-color school map would be easier to memorize, but much harder to defend.

Ken Angrok defeated Kertajaya in 1222 and built authority around Tumapel or Singhasari. Two dated lintels have prompted a recent archaeological argument that he rebuilt a Bameswara-era sanctuary in Kadiri to consolidate rule. That is a reasoned reconstruction from objects and texts, not a filmed palace meeting.

Singhasari records include inscriptions, sculpture, sacred sites, kakawin, and later chronicles that do not always agree. Wisnuwardhana’s commemoration at Jajaghu and Kertanagara’s program show royal power and religious patronage. Conflicts among sources are evidence too; blending them into one smooth thriller would hide the historical problem.

sections.title: See grants, officials, law, and military titles

items.text: Royal inscriptions were formal acts cut on stone or copper and sometimes transmitted through other media. They could name grants, boundaries, taxes, duties, witnesses, and ritual sanctions. Their durability makes government unusually visible, but rulers chose what to record. A charter collection is not an everyday diary or complete constitution.

The 1120 Panumbangan inscription associates Bameswara with a sima grant. Sima status involved specified fiscal privileges and continuing obligations, often linked to service or a sanctuary. Calling it simply “tax-free land” loses the transaction, local duties, named witnesses, and the fact that one grant did not govern every village.

Specialists called citralekha prepared inscriptions with knowledge of Old Javanese language, script, formulae, and court procedure. Their work connected education with administration. A beautifully cut order was not decorative stationery: it could help define land and dues, which made spelling, layout, authentication, and skilled training politically important.

The title tanda appears for elite guards or warriors in Old Javanese inscriptions and literature from Kediri onward. Comparing those genres helps identify a real status without turning every poetic duel into a battle report. Military service, court rank, land, reward, and storytelling overlapped, but their exact relationship could change.

Kediri-period charters name village authorities, religious specialists, craft workers, performers, guards, and other service groups. A 1194 record includes the term walyan for a healer. Such lists reveal recognized roles and administrative categories, but people could combine seasonal, household, ritual, and official work beyond one label.

sections.title: Farm volcanic land and manage Brantas water

items.text: The 1037 Kamalagyan record describes Brantas flooding that damaged fields and hindered boat traffic, then a dam built at Wringin Sapta. The project joined agriculture, transport, royal authority, and local labor. Its inauguration record celebrates action, but does not show every later repair, maintenance burden, or downstream effect.

Old Javanese inscriptions use terms for dams, dikes, reservoirs, tunnels, and channels, and sometimes name officials concerned with water. These structures distributed risk as well as water. Farmers upstream and downstream could need cooperation, negotiation, clearing, and repair, while one broken bank could turn a clever system into a muddy emergency.

Wet-rice cultivation required seedbeds, irrigated fields, draft animals, harvesting, storage, and shared attention to water. Epigraphic research describes village barns and cooperative resources, while also showing variation. “The village” was not one timeless harmonious family; access to land, labor, animals, and authority could be unequal.

The atlas includes Mount Kelud and much of the upper Brantas basin. That map fact helps locate why slopes, river channels, and water works matter, but the polygon is not a farm survey. Inscriptions document particular irrigation structures; they cannot calculate harvests, maintenance burdens, or disaster losses across all four components.

Rice landscapes also depended on people whose names rarely enter royal narratives: households preparing seed, farmers transplanting and harvesting, animal handlers, ditch clearers, and local organizers. Epigraphic terms help recover work and cooperative resources, yet they cannot calculate a typical labor day, wage, diet, or share of the harvest.

sections.title: Connect river routes, ports, and wider Asian seas

items.text: A thirteenth-century Chinese compilation lists rice, pepper, aromatic woods, ivory, metals, silks, ceramics, and other goods in exchanges involving Java. It also describes foreign merchants. The account shows wide maritime networks, but “Java” is broader than this card, and traded objects do not prove one court ruled every port they reached.

The 1178 Lingwai Daida drew information from merchants, sailors, and earlier writing. That helps explain both its value and its blur: port knowledge, traveler reports, and recycled description could sit together. Historians can use its trade and government details without pretending a Chinese author inspected every East Javanese market stall.

Textiles moved as valuable goods, gifts, payments, and status markers. Sea routes linked Indonesian waters through Malacca toward India and the western Indian Ocean, while sculpted patterns preserve local artistic choices rather than shipping records. No carved design can supply one merchant’s name, exact route, price, or wearer’s biography.

The Brantas connected fields and inland movement to boat traffic, yet the atlas polygon excludes tested Sidoarjo or Janggala, Surabaya, Gresik, and Tuban. That is a striking cartographic weakness for a story involving river and maritime exchange. A map can color Bima and still miss key East Javanese delta and coast points.

Kertanagara pursued a more outward-looking Singhasari policy, including a 1275 expedition toward Malayu in the card’s final years. Material evidence for a grand island-wide program remains limited. Maritime ambition mattered, but the atlas’s Borneo and Bima components are not proof that Singhasari ruled those places in 1279.

sections.title: Read inscriptions, poetry, performance, and learning

items.text: Writing sample from the Old Javanese face of the Pucangan charter, dated 6 November 1041: scholarly transliteration “svasti śaka-varṣātīta 963 kārtika-māsa”; translation, “Hail! Elapsed Śaka year 963, month of Kārttika.” It was written in Kawi script. Original carved glyphs are not reproduced because modern Unicode text would not be a facsimile.

The 1135 Hantang stone preserves the short formula “pañjalu jayati,” translated “Panjalu is victorious,” in a quadrate script context. It is a securely attested royal sample and an excellent two-word boast. It is not an everyday conversation, proof that everyone read, or enough evidence to reconstruct the entire battle.

Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh completed the Bharatayuddha in 1157 under Jayabhaya’s patronage. They transformed Mahabharata material into Old Javanese kakawin using demanding meters, language, and court knowledge. This was creative intellectual work. “Based on another epic” is very different from “copied without thinking.”

Kediri-era kakawin survived largely through later manuscript traditions, especially in Bali. A palm-leaf copy can be centuries younger than the composition, and scribes may preserve, adjust, or explain language. Historians therefore separate the date of a poem, the date of a surviving copy, performance history, and modern edition.

Advanced learning is visible in poets and citralekha who mastered scripts, meters, and formulae. Outside that narrow record, children may have learned work, stories, ritual, and crafts by participating with adults, but this is a cautious reconstruction. No consulted source supplies a school age, timetable, enrollment rate, or literacy percentage.

sections.title: Build sanctuaries, carve stone, and practice religion

items.text: Tondowongso preserves a brick sanctuary complex with an eleventh- to thirteenth-century horizon. Its plan, sculpture, and construction reveal organized labor and skilled craft, but individual phases remain difficult to date. A ritual compound is excellent architecture evidence and a terrible blueprint for the average family’s bedroom or bathroom.

Tondowongso and Gurah finds include Brahma, Candra, Surya, Nandi, and a yoni. Their materials, iconography, carving, and archaeological contexts help researchers study craft and worship, while investigation remains unfinished. They document particular sacred settings, not one uniform East Javanese religion, and cannot reveal how often an ordinary farmer visited.

The 1197 Palah inscription invokes King Srnga at a sacred place later called Panataran. Most prominent surviving monuments there belong to later Majapahit phases. The early text proves a twelfth-century sacred connection, not that Kertajaya commissioned every tower now standing. Buildings can outlive, expand beyond, and confuse dynasties.

At Keboireng, researchers combine a distinctive kala ornament, the Mula Malurung inscription, and a Kapulungan place-name to argue for a Bhairawa sanctuary in a Singhasari setting. The method is as interesting as the answer: art, text, and landscape must agree. Even then, one sanctuary cannot define everyone’s belief.

Singhasari-period sculpture under Kertanagara includes finely carved textile patterns and elaborate ornaments. A study of sumping ear ornaments traces both convention and artistic choice, while Jajaghu commemorated Wisnuwardhana. These works show patronage and virtuoso carving. Sacred or royal stone fashion was not the muddy-field dress code.

sections.title: Meet families, ranks, women, and children cautiously

items.text: Old Javanese kakawin depict marriage by arrangement, elopement or abduction, kinship, longing, and elaborate ceremony. Those themes mattered to audiences, but elite literary couples are not a census. The particular Subhadrawiwaha studied is later, so it can illuminate a tradition without being backdated into every eleventh-century household.

Inscriptions reveal kings, officials, religious specialists, village authorities, farmers, artisans, guards, performers, dependent workers, and healers. Rank shaped duties, access, and reward, while a person’s work could cross categories. Administrative lists preserve labels better than feelings, so they cannot tell how each family negotiated status or hardship.

Women appear in court marriage stories, textile labor, exchange, household production, and ritual, but direct biographies outside royal circles are rare. Elite heroines cannot represent all women, and silence in a king’s inscription is not absence from fields or markets. Evidence supports participation more securely than one universal gender script.

Village labor and specialist scribes give bounded clues to childhood. Children may have watched adults, carried small tasks, practiced crafts, memorized stories or ritual, tended animals, or entered specialist training, but this remains a cautious reconstruction. The sources supply no standard childhood timetable, school, or equally gentle workload.

Later Panji traditions center love, separation, disguise, kinship, and rival Janggala and Panjalu courts, then spread across languages and regions. Their families are memorable because stories kept changing. They are cultural afterlives, not literal biographies, and certainly not proof that every parent solved teenage drama with a royal quest.

sections.title: Eat, dress, live, work, and find amusement

items.text: Twelfth-century poetry preserves an early detailed description of rice partly boiled and then finished in a bamboo steamer. It also discusses breakfast and feast food. These are valuable clues to technique and vocabulary, but poetic kitchens use metaphor and elite settings. They do not prove one breakfast menu for every village.

A Chinese account lists rice, millet, beans, gourds, coconut, banana, sugarcane, taro, fish, fowl, ducks, goats, and sea-boiled salt for Java. That is a regional abundance list, not a shopping basket. Season, class, religion, ecology, and household means shaped what anyone actually ate on an ordinary day.

Cloth could be work, wealth, gift, payment, trade, and visible rank. Texts and sculpture preserve fine names and patterns, while fibers and ordinary garments survive poorly. Jewelry and sumping carved on sacred figures reveal artistic vocabulary. They do not mean everyone weeded rice wearing stone-statue accessories, which sounds exhausting.

The consulted Tondowongso evidence supplies a brick ritual plan, not a domestic one. It cannot let us tour an ordinary family’s rooms, assign one standard household layout, or compare urban and rural housing. The honest reconstruction is a gap in this source base, not a temple remodeled into a home.

Charters name village authorities, craft workers, performers, guards, healers, and other service groups. Chinese reporting adds merchants and describes music, mime, outings, and animal contests. These amusements may reflect elite or regional practice. No one should schedule every child for a royal pig fight after chores.

sections.title: Ask about medicine, water, toilets, and the 1279 ending

items.text: The 1194 Kemulan inscription includes walyan, interpreted as a healer, among named occupational specialists. A Chinese Java account also mentions healing, but at regional outsider scale. Together they support the presence of healers, not a recipe book. Treatment, training, effectiveness, fees, childbirth care, and access remain largely unknown.

Brantas dams and channels supported irrigation, transport, and flood control, but those systems are not household drinking-water evidence. Field water, bathing, wells, and domestic storage are different questions. Consulted sources do not securely describe routine boiling, contamination testing, or equal access to safe water across the polygon.

No consulted source securely identifies a typical household toilet, sewer network, garbage service, or handwashing rule for this period. Tondowongso documents a ritual complex, so its plan cannot be reassigned to an imaginary family bathroom. The honest toilet tour has one stop: “evidence missing; please mind the gap.”

Kediri lost political dominance in 1222 and Singhasari followed, but a dynastic transition is not evidence that residents or settlements vanished. Panji traditions later carried Janggala and Panjalu settings far beyond East Java. Political authority changed; later cultural memory should not be mistaken for the same state quietly surviving under a new logo.

At 1279 the atlas ends east-java and assigns the same eleven tested member points to kediri. Historically, Kediri had fallen in 1222 and Singhasari continued until 1292 under Kertanagara. This seam is neither a fall nor a valid successor event, and it cannot date changes in people, language, work, worship, or landscape.

ending.text: At the 1279 snapshot, the exact east-java id disappears and the atlas relabels all eleven tested member points as kediri. Historical Kediri had lost independent dominance in 1222, while Singhasari continued under Kertanagara until 1292, and the atlas has no exact singhasari record. Nothing in the cited chronology marks 1279 as a conquest, collapse, or community break. This is an editorial seam, so the override leaves fell null and invents no successor event.
